references.text: Describes the actual event the woman refers to in verse 13: the serpent deceived her, and she ate from the fruit.
Paul directly references the serpent's deception of Eve: 'The serpent deceived Eve with his cunning' – a direct echo of הִשִּׁיאַנִי (he deceived me) in Gen 3:13.
Paul writes that it was not Adam who was deceived, but the woman who was deceived and fell into transgression – a direct reference to Gen 3:13.
Paul explains how sin entered the world through one man (Adam), a consequence of the fall described in Gen 3.
Revelation identifies Satan as 'the ancient serpent, who deceives the whole world' – a direct reference to the serpent that deceived the woman in Gen 3:13.
Again, the dragon is identified as 'the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan,' linking back to the serpent in Genesis 3.
A direct narrative connection showing cause (temptation) and effect (sin and defense) in the fall of man.
Theological contrast between the unity of creation (Gen 2:23) and the rupture caused by the fall (Gen 3:13).
A direct narrative connection showing the development of dialogue in the fall of man.
Theological contrast between the serpent as tempter (Gen 3) and the serpent as an instrument of judgment (Num 21).
Theological contrast between imputation of guilt (Gen 3:13) and personal accountability (2 Sam 24:17).
